title: Why say what you don't do?
hookLine: why do you say what you do not do (61:2–3)

lines: WORDS THAT FLOAT AHEAD OF DEEDS.
cards: We'll grab coffee soon. I'll send you that link. Let me look into it.
I'll call Mom this weekend. A busy week leaves a trail of these behind it, said warmly, meant at the time, then lost. Nobody's lying exactly.

The words just float off ahead of the deeds and never get caught up with. Right after its first verse of praise, Surah sixty-one asks a question aimed straight at that gap, and the people it asks first are the believers.

teach.b: Verses two and three. Pickthall: "O ye who believe! Why say ye that which ye do not? It is most hateful in the sight of Allah that ye say that which ye do not." In Arabic: lima taquluna ma la taf'alun.
The sound carries the sting: taquluna, you say; taf'alun, you do. The two verbs end alike, and the verse asks why the deeds don't match the words.
Then a strong word: kabura maqtan. Maqt is intense dislike, disgust, and the verse calls this gap grave in God's sight.
Commentators record that some believers had said, if only we knew which deeds God loves most, we'd do them. Then, when a hard task was asked, some held back.
The verse catches them in the space between the boast and the moment. The Qur'an returns to this theme.

teach.h: SHU'AYB: I DO WHAT I ASK.
teach.b: In Surah Hud, the prophet Shu'ayb tells his people he doesn't want to go behind their backs and do what he forbids them. He won't ask of them what he won't do himself.
In Surah Al-Baqarah, people are asked: do you command others to righteousness and forget yourselves? The point is not to stop speaking about the good. It's to close the gap.

teach.h: PROMISE LESS, DO WHAT YOU PROMISE.
teach.b: One practical reading: promise less, and do what you promise.

how: Muslim teachers often cite 61:2–3 when speaking about keeping promises and matching speech to action; many Muslims add in sha' Allah, if God wills, when promising something for the future.

o: a broken promise that must be paid back
a lie told on purpose to deceive others
intense dislike, a strong word of disapproval

games.q: say and do — tap the pairs.

s: the two verbs in the question end with the same sound
taquluna, you say; taf'alun, you do: alike in sound, apart in practice.
commentators link the verse to people who boasted they'd do the most loved deeds, then held back
the verse catches the space between the boast and the moment.
the verse tells believers to stop speaking about good things
the point is to close the gap between word and deed.

games.q: some believers say: if only we knew the deeds God loves most, we'd do them. then a hard task comes. what does the verse ask?
o: why do you say what you don't do?
who among you is the bravest?
games.why: it asks why they say what they don't do, and calls the gap grave in God's sight.

practice: Scroll back, in your mind, through the last week or two, and find one thing you said you'd do and haven't: a call, a favor, a returned item. Picture yourself doing it, start to finish.
Notice any small embarrassment and let it go on the out-breath; the deed closes the gap better than guilt does.

wordCard.voice: Maqt: intense dislike, disgust, the word Surah As-Saff uses for the gap between what believers say and what they do. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: why do you say what you do not do? The two verbs rhyme, and the verse asks why they don't match.

carryVoice: Your line: say it, do it. Fewer promises, and the kept kind. Six hundred twenty-four, in the books.
